acer-platanoides-crimson-king.note: Planted for a century and now a problem in the woods. Ask before you plant another.

acer-rubrum-autumn-blaze.note: Fast growing; wants room for the crown.

acer-saccharum-green-mountain.note: The tree a whole autumn is about. Give it the room it will want in forty years.

achillea-millefolium-paprika.note: Native to the roadsides here and just as happy in a border; it flops in rich soil.

adiantum-pedatum.note: Black stems and a horseshoe of leaflets. It wants the soil of a forest floor.

ajuga-reptans.note: Blue spikes over bronze leaves, and it will walk into the lawn if you let it.

allium-globemaster.note: A globe the size of a child's ball on a stem that stands all summer, even dry.

allium-schoenoprasum.note: Cut it and it comes back. The flowers are edible and the bees like them too.

amelanchier-canadensis.note: Blossom, then berries the birds take about four minutes before you do.

amsonia-tabernaemontana.note: Blue in May and butter yellow in October, out of the same leaves.

andropogon-gerardii.note: The grass the prairie was made of. Too big for a small border and right for a big one.

anethum-graveolens.note: Sow it every year, and let one stand for the swallowtails.

artemisia-schmidtiana.note: A silver dome that has to be cut back the moment it opens in the middle.

asclepias-incarnata.note: The wet corner's answer to the last one, and just as good for caterpillars.

asclepias-tuberosa.note: The monarch caterpillar needs the plant, and the plant wants sand and sun.

astilbe-arendsii-fanal.note: The shade plant that flowers rather than merely coping.

athyrium-filix-femina.note: The easy fern: fine-textured, quick, and it seeds itself about gently.

baptisia-australis.note: Blue spikes in June and black pods after, and it resents being moved.

betula-nigra-heritage.note: The birch for a wet corner: it shrugs off the borers that take the paper birch.

betula-papyrifera.note: Borer prone; keep the root zone cool and shaded.

buddleja-davidii.note: The butterflies do come. Cut it to the ground in spring, and check it is not on your local problem list before you plant it.

buxus-sempervirens.note: Shears into any shape; grown for its foliage.

calamagrostis-acutiflora-karl-foerster.note: It stands up in a storm, which is the whole reason it is everywhere.

callicarpa-bodinieri-profusion.note: The berries arrive in October and are a colour nothing else in the garden has.

caryopteris-clandonensis-blue-mist.note: Late blue when the border has run out of ideas. Cut it back in spring.

chrysanthemum-sheffield.note: A mum that comes back every year, which is not true of the ones sold in pots.

clematis-jackmanii.note: Cool feet and a warm head: shade the roots and give it the sun, or it sulks.

clethra-alnifolia-hummingbird.note: Spice in the air in August, and bees in the whole plant while it lasts.

coleus-scutellarioides.note: Grown for the leaf, and it will take shade a flower will not.

coreopsis-verticillata-moonbeam.note: A pale yellow that reads as light rather than as colour.

cornus-alba-elegantissima.note: Variegated leaf, red stem, and the same rule: cut it back or lose the colour.

cornus-alternifolia.note: Horizontal branches under a flat crown; it reads as a small tree even in leaf.

cornus-sericea.note: The stems are the winter show and they are only red on young wood, so cut a third to the ground each spring.

cosmos-bipinnatus.note: An annual: it is sown, it blooms, and it is composted. Nothing to overwinter.

crocus-vernus.note: The first thing the bees find, in a snow-melt week.

deschampsia-cespitosa.note: A grass that takes both the shade and the wet, which almost no other grass will.

dryopteris-erythrosora.note: New croziers come up copper and fade to green.

echinacea-purpurea-magnus.note: Leave the cones standing and it seeds itself into a colony for the birds.

echinops-bannaticus.note: Blue globes on grey stems, and the bees are on them before they are fully open.

enkianthus-campanulatus.note: Bells in spring, scarlet in October, and it wants the same acid ground as a rhododendron.

eutrochium-purpureum.note: Two metres of dusty pink and every bee in the county. Give it the back of the border.

fothergilla-gardenii.note: Bottlebrush flowers before the leaves and a three-colour autumn after them.

gaillardia-grandiflora-goblin.note: Hot, dry and poor is what it wants. Coddle it and it dies over the winter.

galanthus-nivalis.note: Flowers while the ground is still frozen. Plant it where you walk past in February.

geranium-maculatum.note: A native that seeds itself quietly into the shade under a shrub.

geranium-rozanne.note: Flowers from June to the frost, which nothing else in this list manages without a rest.

gleditsia-triacanthos-inermis-sunburst.note: Thin shade, so the lawn survives under it, and it takes the worst of a boulevard.

hakonechloa-macra-aureola.note: It spills over a wall like water, and it is grown for the leaf rather than a plume.

hamamelis-virginiana.note: The last flower of the year, opening as the leaves come down, when nothing else is doing anything at all.

helenium-autumnale-moerheim-beauty.note: Copper and rust in September, when the rest of the palette has gone quiet.

helleborus-niger.note: Blooms across the new year, which is why the bloom set is circular.

hemerocallis-stella-de-oro.note: One flower a day for six weeks, and not a lily at all.

heuchera-palace-purple.note: Heaves out of the ground in a freeze-thaw winter; mulch after the ground sets.

hibiscus-syriacus.note: Late, showy, and it seeds itself about if you let it.

hosta-patriot.note: Slug damage is the whole story of a hosta bed.

hydrangea-anomala-petiolaris.note: Nothing for three years, then it covers the wall. Plant it and be patient.

hydrangea-arborescens-annabelle.note: Flops in a thunderstorm unless it is cut to the ground every March.

hydrangea-macrophylla-endless-summer.note: Blue in acid ground and pink in lime, and the colour is the soil's doing rather than the plant's. It flowers on old wood and new, which is why it survives a bad spring.

hydrangea-paniculata-limelight.note: Blooms on new wood, so it may be cut back hard in spring.

hydrangea-quercifolia.note: Oak-shaped leaves and a red autumn that nothing else in the border does.

hylotelephium-autumn-joy.note: Carries the border into October and then stands there, brown and dry, all winter.

impatiens-walleriana.note: Flowers in the shade all summer. Downy mildew took the old ones out of the trade, so ask for a resistant series.

iris-sibirica.note: Takes wet ground in spring and dry ground in August, which is most of this climate.

itea-virginica-henrys-garnet.note: A wet-corner shrub that turns crimson: two reasons to plant it, which is one more than most.

juniperus-chinensis-pfitzeriana.note: Half a century of parking-lot planting has not made it any less useful.

juniperus-scopulorum-blue-arrow.note: A blue pencil for a narrow bed, and it holds the colour through winter.

kalmia-latifolia.note: A sturdier evergreen for acid ground than most rhododendrons, and the buds alone are worth it.

lamprocapnos-spectabilis.note: Flowers in May and disappears in July. Put something in front of the hole it leaves.

leucanthemum-superbum-becky.note: The white daisy a child draws, and it stays upright in rain.

liatris-spicata.note: Flowers from the top down, which is the wrong way round and looks deliberate.

lilium-stargazer.note: Scented enough to fill a room, and the one bulb the deer will eat to the ground.

lonicera-sempervirens.note: A twiner, not a cling-er: it needs a trellis or a wire.

malus-royalty.note: Purple leaf, dark flowers, and scab in a wet June. Choose it for the leaf, not the fruit.

matteuccia-struthiopteris.note: The fiddleheads are edible in May; after that it is a two-metre vase of fronds.

mentha-spicata.note: Put it in a pot, or it owns the bed within two seasons.

miscanthus-sinensis-morning-light.note: The plume is the winter and the plant is the summer. Cut it down in March, never in autumn.

monarda-didyma-jacob-cline.note: The hummingbird plant. Give it moving air or mildew takes it by August.

muscari-armeniacum.note: Blue in the lawn before the first cut, and it multiplies where it is happy.

narcissus-carlton.note: Leave the foliage six weeks after flowering; only then cut it.

nepeta-faassenii.note: Six weeks of grey-blue haze, then shear it and get six more. The cat will roll in it either way.

ocimum-basilicum-genovese.note: An annual in this climate whatever the label says. Pinch the flowers or the leaves go bitter.

origanum-vulgare.note: Poor soil makes the flavour; a rich bed makes leaves and no oil.

paeonia-lactiflora-festiva-maxima.note: Wants a cold winter and its crown an inch under the soil. Planted too deep it sulks for years.

panicum-virgatum-northwind.note: Stands up through the winter; cut down in late spring, not autumn.

parthenocissus-quinquefolia.note: Crimson in October on a wall nothing else would cover. It holds on with little cups, not roots.

pelargonium-hortorum.note: The window-box plant, and it wants to dry out a little between waterings.

pennisetum-alopecuroides-hameln.note: Soft bottlebrush plumes, and the seed heads hold the frost in the morning.

perovskia-atriplicifolia.note: Silver stems and blue haze in the hottest, poorest bed you have.

petroselinum-crispum.note: A biennial: the second year it flowers and stops being parsley.

petunia-atkinsiana.note: Trailing ones fill a basket by July and want deadheading as much as water.

phlox-paniculata-david.note: White, fragrant, and the one garden phlox that resists mildew. Plant it where air moves.

phlox-subulata-emerald-cushion.note: A sheet of colour in April on a bank nothing else will hold.

physocarpus-opulifolius-diabolo.note: Dark leaf, tough as a fence post, and native to the edge of a swamp.

picea-glauca-densata.note: The spruce for a windbreak: dense, tough, and it does not mind the cold end of the map.

picea-pungens-hoopsii.note: Blue, slow, and the best of the blue spruces for a small yard.

polystichum-acrostichoides.note: Evergreen through the winter, which is why it is the fern for a north wall.

potentilla-fruticosa-goldfinger.note: Flowers from June to frost and asks for nothing: the prairie answer to a rose.

prunus-virginiana-shubert.note: A native that colours like a plum. It suckers, so plant it where a thicket is welcome.

quercus-rubra.note: Fast for an oak, and the acorns come at thirty. A tree for the next owner of the house.

rhododendron-pjm.note: It needs acid ground; everything else about it is easy.

rosa-knock-out.note: Black spot barely bothers it and it flowers until the snow: the rose for people who gave up on roses.

rosa-rugosa.note: Salt, sand and wind, and it still sets hips. Plant it where nothing else will grow.

rosmarinus-officinalis.note: A shrub where it is hardy and a pot you bring inside here. Pinch it or it goes woody.

rudbeckia-fulgida-goldsturm.note: Divide every third spring or the centre dies out.

salix-integra-hakuro-nishiki.note: Pink and white on every new shoot, which means it is dullest exactly when it is oldest.

salvia-nemorosa-caradonna.note: Cut it back after the first flush and it does the whole thing again in September.

salvia-officinalis.note: Cut back by a third in spring; it goes woody if left.

schizachyrium-scoparium.note: Blue-green in June, rust in October, and it holds that colour under snow.

sedum-spurium-john-creech.note: A mat of pink in July that keeps the weeds out of everything underneath it.

solidago-fireworks.note: Goldenrod does not cause your hay fever; the ragweed beside it does.

sorghastrum-nutans.note: Gold in September; plant it where it can stand against the sky.

spiraea-japonica-gold-mound.note: The low gold-leaf spirea: clip it and it flowers again.

stachys-byzantina.note: The leaves are the point. Pinch the flowers off and it stays a carpet.

syringa-meyeri-palibin.note: A lilac for a small yard: fragrant, and it takes a hard cut without sulking.

syringa-reticulata.note: The lilac that is a tree. Cream plumes in June, and no mildew worth mentioning.

syringa-vulgaris.note: Blooms on last year's wood: prune after flowering, never in spring.

tagetes-patula.note: Cheap, tough, and it flowers until the frost takes it.

taxus-cuspidata.note: The one evergreen that will take the north side of a house. Every part of it is toxic, so keep it out of a fence line a dog patrols.

thuja-occidentalis-hetz-midget.note: A globe that stays a globe: evergreen without a hedge to clip.

thuja-occidentalis-smaragd.note: Grown for its foliage; none of the catalogue's conifers bloom on a schedule.

thymus-serpyllum.note: Wants sharp drainage; dies in a wet winter clay.

thymus-vulgaris.note: The kitchen needs it and the bees use it; it wants sand and no kindness.

tiarella-cordifolia.note: Foam over the leaves in May, and it spreads itself politely.

tulipa-queen-of-night.note: Nearly black in the vase and purple in the sun. Plant them deep and let the leaves yellow.

viburnum-carlesii.note: The most fragrant thing in this catalogue in April.

viburnum-trilobum.note: Berries for the birds and a red autumn: a hedge that earns its place.

waldsteinia-fragarioides.note: Yellow flowers and no fruit, but it does the job under a shrub.

weigela-florida-wine-and-roses.note: Dark leaf and pink flower, and the hummingbirds find it before you do.

wisteria-frutescens.note: The native wisteria: slower than the Asian ones and far less likely to take the downspout with it.

zinnia-elegans.note: Cut it and it flowers harder. Powdery mildew gets it if the air stands still.
